components.text: Whether the proposed historical core rests on sufficiently reliable and independently supported source material.
Whether the proposed appearance facts rest on a sufficiently reliable historical record.
Whether scholarly agreement on a list of facts supplies adequate independent evidential support.
Whether any important resurrection tradition is early and linked closely enough to named witnesses to mitigate the record limitations.
Whether early Pauline tradition provides source proximity despite the broader record's limitations.
Whether the tradition can be linked to eyewitness-associated figures Peter and James.
Whether the reported disciple experiences require an external bodily object rather than an ordinary psychological explanation.
Whether the disciples' appearance experiences require an external risen body as their object.
Whether grief-related experiences offer an ordinary explanation of the reported appearances.
Whether grief visions plausibly fit the relevant subjects, groups, circumstances, and resulting transformations.
Whether there is affirmative historical evidence for the psychological conditions attributed to Paul and the disciples.
Whether grief hallucinations fit the relevant disciples and reported circumstances.
Whether the proposed psychological account can also explain Paul and the diversity of cases.
Whether rejecting specific psychological reconstructions is enough to establish a publicly observable physical resurrection.
Whether the reported experiences warrant an external, visible, and photographable body rather than a restrained interpretation.
Whether early tradition overcomes the large residual ignorance surrounding the event and its interpretation.
Whether failure of particular psychological theories warrants the positive resurrection inference.
Whether limited evidence can distinguish an externally visible physical body from a tentative natural interpretation.
Whether the appearance evidence establishes physical contact rather than merely reported seeing or an invitation to touch.
Whether an appearance report by itself supplies evidence of an externally tangible body.
Whether transformative appearance experiences generally establish a bodily encounter.
Whether the broader resurrection narratives report actual sensory and physical interaction despite ambiguity about Thomas's completed touch.
Whether the reports include tangible, shared bodily features inconsistent with a merely ghostly grief experience.
Whether the evidence supports a physical body visible and tangible to observers.
Whether the textual tradition contains affirmative seeing and touching evidence despite the Thomas ambiguity.
Whether the traditions describe a tangible physical body rather than an unobservable manifestation.
Whether the claimed resurrection body is conceptually coherent when it is also characterized as spiritual or immaterial.
Whether the proposed resurrection body is conceptually coherent when also described as spiritual.
Whether calling something immaterial supplies characteristics compatible with genuine embodiment.
Whether Paul's phrase spiritual body means an immaterial or wispy spirit and is therefore internally incoherent.
Whether Pauline language supports a transformed physical body rather than an entirely nonphysical manifestation.
Whether Paul's spiritual-body language entails an immaterial or disembodied entity.
Whether Philippians 3 supplies a positive transformed-body interpretation that defeats the alleged incoherence.
Whether coherent bodily language alone makes miracle belief rational independently of a person's justified antecedent beliefs.
Whether sensory reports rationally require a miraculous conclusion for an observer whose prior expectation favors error.
Whether appearance reports have the same rational force under materially different antecedent beliefs.
Whether Pauline spiritual-body language coherently denotes transformed physical embodiment.
Whether the asserted empty tomb distinguishes resurrection from ordinary removal given the absence of independent witnesses.
Whether uncertainty about disposition of the body undermines the independently supported premise that crucifixion caused death.
Whether appearance reports determine what happened to the body.
Whether the empty-tomb evidence excludes ordinary removal of the body.
Whether the available witnesses and distant record permit a reliable reconstruction of the body's disposition.
Whether merely possible body-removal accounts explain the evidence as well as a unified resurrection hypothesis.
Whether one hallucination account can explain both Paul and the disciples.
Whether restraint alone answers the comparative explanatory demand posed by the combined evidence.
Whether merely possible body removals explain the evidential set as a unified whole.
Whether one grief-hallucination account fits both Paul and the disciples.
Whether historical restraint alone answers the comparative explanatory demand.
Whether the con side must provide one satisfactory complete naturalistic reconstruction before resurrection remains unestablished.
Whether hallucination explains the empty tomb evidence.
Whether hallucination can explain a substantial portion of the appearance evidence despite acknowledged residual gaps.
Whether rejecting resurrection requires a satisfactory complete naturalistic reconstruction.
Whether hallucination may retain partial explanatory value despite leaving the empty tomb unexplained.
Whether there is independent background evidence capable of raising the prior plausibility of resurrection.
Whether anomalous and survival evidence supplies a comparative answer to incomplete natural alternatives.
Whether background evidence can rationally alter initially skeptical miracle priors.
Whether evidence for God, present anomalies, and survival makes resurrection antecedently less improbable.
Whether sufficiently rich convergent identification and interaction evidence can warrant resurrection despite incomplete natural alternatives.
Whether spectacular enough evidence can overcome the ordinary prior presumption that a dead person remains dead.
Whether bodily identification evidence can reduce generic removal or substitution possibilities.
Whether sufficiently rich positive evidence can establish resurrection without demanding a complete natural rival.
Whether identification and multiple-witness evidence can overcome the ordinary presumption of continued death.
Whether the proposed background case supplies justified beliefs about a supernatural agent's existence, nature, and intentions.
Whether convergent anomaly evidence identifies a miracle's agent and purpose rather than merely an unexplained event.
Whether generic background anomalies suffice without justified beliefs about a supernatural agent.
Whether unexplained convergent evidence can rationally be attributed specifically to miraculous agency.
Whether the alleged resurrection is connected to a specific theological tradition, claimant identity, and divine intention.
Whether the proposed miracle can be connected to a specific supernatural agent and intention.
Whether Jesus' claims and Mosaic-theistic context provide an authentication framework for resurrection.
